lessons.introText: When a silent e sits at the end of a word, it reaches back over one consonant and makes the vowel before it say its own name. Say each word out loud and listen for the long /ā/ sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: E_e is the rarest of the silent-e patterns, but it works the same way as the others: the quiet e makes the vowel say its name, /ē/. Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In an i_e word, the silent e turns a short i into the long i sound, /ī/. Say each word out loud and listen for the vowel saying its own name.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Just like a_e, an o_e word keeps a silent e at the end so the o says its name, /ō/. Say each word out loud and listen for the long o.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: U_e can spell two different sounds — the /yoo/ in "cute" or the /oo/ in "flute" — so listen closely to each word as you say it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Shr blends three sounds smoothly into one: /s/ + /h/ + /r/. Say each word out loud and listen for that blended start.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Thr combines /th/ and /r/ right at the front of a word. Say each word out loud and listen for the blend.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In sch words, the h is silent and the whole team of letters just makes the /sk/ sound. Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When w comes before ar, it changes the vowel's sound completely — ar after w usually says /or/, as in "war" and "warm." Say each word out loud and listen closely.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: W also changes the sound of or — wor usually says /er/, as in "worm" and "world." Say each word out loud and listen for that twist.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: The ending -or often names a person who does something, like an actor or a visitor, and it says a quiet, unstressed /er/ sound. Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: -Er is the most common way to spell the /er/ sound at the end of a word, as in "camper" and "teacher." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Old is a steady spelling pattern — the o keeps its long sound even in front of two consonants. Say each word out loud and listen for the long o.

sentences: It is cold
so hold my hand.
The old dog was bold and gold.
She sold and told us not to be cold.
Do not scold me for the mold.
I will fold my old
gold shirt.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Like old, oll keeps its long o sound, as in "roll" and "stroll." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: I will roll the doll down the hill.
We took a stroll by the toll road.
She read the scroll at the poll.
A troll sat on the knoll.
Roll the doll to the top of the knoll.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Olt belongs to the same long-o family as old and oll. Say each word out loud and listen for the long o before "lt."

sentences: The bolt fell with a jolt.
The colt will molt this spring.
That volt of power gave me a jolt.
Do not call him a dolt.
The colt ran fast after the jolt.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oth usually keeps the long o sound, as in "both" — though a few words in this family can also say a short o, so listen carefully to each one.

sentences: Both the moth and the sloth are slow.
I spilled broth on the cloth.
The moth flew near the cloth.
A sloth ate broth for lunch.
Both animals liked the warm broth.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Most ost words say a long o, as in "most" and "toast," but a couple of common exceptions (like "cost") do not — say each word out loud and listen for which sound it uses.

sentences: Most kids like toast in the morning.
The host put up a post by the coast.
I am almost done with my roast.
A ghost sat by the mail post.
We ate roast and toast on the coast.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ind usually keeps its long i sound, as in "find" and "kind." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: I will find my kind
blind dog.
Please remind me to wind the clock.
Do you mind if I sit behind you?
The wind will grind the old leaves.
Be kind and remind your friend.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ild is a short but dependable long-i pattern, as in "child" and "wild." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: The child was mild and kind.
A wild dog ran by the child.
It was a mild day for the child to play.
The wild wind did not scare the child.
That child likes wild and mild days.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ull says the short /oo/ sound, as in "full" and "pull." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: The cup is full of water.
Pull the bull to the barn.
I fully filled the full cup.
The bull did not want to pull.
We pull and fill it up full.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ush also uses that short /oo/-ish sound, as in "push" and "rush." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: Push the bush out of the way.
Hush now
do not rush.
The mush made me blush.
Water will gush and flush the sink.
Do not rush or push your friend.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: The suffix -ful means "full of" and is always spelled with just one l, even though it sounds like it could have two. Say each word out loud and listen for the ending.

sentences: Be careful and helpful today.
The playful dog is hopeful for a treat.
This tool is useful and helpful.
I am thankful for my careful friend.
She is hopeful and thankful too.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: All keeps its own steady sound no matter which letter comes before it, as in "ball" and "small." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: I will call you at the mall.
The ball hit the tall wall.
We will fall down the hall.
A small ball rolled by the wall.
Call me if you fall at the mall.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ai spells the long a sound in the middle of a word or syllable, as in "rain" and "train." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ay spells that same long a sound, but at the end of a word, as in "play" and "day." Ai and ay are a team — just used in different spots. Say each word out loud and listen.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ee is the most common way to spell the long e sound, as in "tree" and "sweet." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a word, ey can also spell the long e sound, as in "key" and "money." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ea often spells the long e sound, as in "beach" and "read." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ea can surprise you — in these words it spells short e instead, as in "bread" and "head." Say each word out loud and listen for the different sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In just a handful of words, ea unexpectedly spells long a, as in "great" and "break." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ie usually spells the long e sound, as in "field" and "chief" — think of the old rule "i before e." Say each word out loud and listen.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a word, ie can also spell long i, as in "pie" and "tie." Say each word out loud and listen for the different sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Aw spells the /aw/ sound, usually at the end of a word or syllable, as in "saw" and "paw." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Au spells that same /aw/ sound, but in the middle of a word, as in "sauce" and "autumn." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oa spells the long o sound in the middle of a word, as in "boat" and "coat." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oe spells the long o sound at the end of a word, as in "toe" and "Joe." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ow can spell the long o sound, as in "snow" and "grow." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ue spells the long u sound, as in "glue" and "blue." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ew also spells the long u sound, as in "new" and "grew." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ow can also spell a completely different sound, the /ow/ diphthong, as in "cow" and "town." Same letters, new sound — say each word out loud and listen closely.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ou spells that same /ow/ diphthong, as in "cloud" and "sound." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oi spells the /oy/ diphthong in the middle of a word, as in "coin" and "oil." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oy spells that same /oy/ sound, but at the end of a word, as in "boy" and "toy." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oo can spell a long, breathy /oo/ sound, as in "moon" and "food." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Oo can also spell a shorter sound, as in "book" and "look" — the very same two letters making a different sound. Say each word out loud and listen closely.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In the middle of a word, y often acts like a short i, as in "gym" and "myth." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: We go to the gym to hear the myth.
This system is not like the gym.
The myth is about the gym system.
I like the gym and the myth story.
Our system at the gym is new.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a short word, y usually says long i, as in "fly" and "sky." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: I will try to fly in the sky.
Do not cry
the sky is dry.
Why is my shy dog crying?
The fly went dry in my sky.
Try not to be shy in the sky.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a longer word, y usually says long e instead, as in "happy" and "candy." Say each word out loud and listen for the difference.

sentences: The happy baby is at the party.
I am sleepy after eating candy.
That funny baby makes me happy.
We had candy at the funny party.
The sleepy baby is happy now.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: The prefix a- at the start of a word is usually said quickly and softly, like /uh/, as in "awake" and "about." Say each word out loud and listen for that quiet beginning.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When c is followed by e, i, or y, it softens and says /s/ instead of its usual hard sound, as in "cent" and "city." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When g is followed by e, i, or y, it can soften to say /j/, as in "page" and "giant." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Dge also spells the /j/ sound, and it always follows a short vowel, as in "bridge" and "judge." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In many words, gh is completely silent — you just don't hear it at all, as in "night" and "light." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentences: The light is bright at night.
I will fight for what is right.
The bird flew high with a sigh.
At eight
the night is bright.
Fight for the right
bright light.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In a smaller group of words, gh actually says /f/, as in "laugh" and "tough." Say each word out loud and listen for the surprise sound.

sentences: I laugh at the rough
tough game.
That cough is enough for today.
The rough road made me laugh.
Enough laughing
my cough is tough.
It was a rough day
but I laugh enough.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In some words borrowed from Greek, ch says /k/ instead of its usual sound, as in "school" and "chorus." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: The chorus sang at school today.
The chemist played a chord on the piano.
An echo came from the school chorus.
The chord had a nice echo.
At school
the chemist sang in the chorus.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Ch usually makes its familiar sound at the start of a word, as in "church" and "cheese." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When k comes right before n at the start of a word, the k stays completely silent, as in "knee" and "knife." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When w comes right before r at the start of a word, the w stays silent, as in "write" and "wrist." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentences: I wrote the wrong word on my wrist.
Wrap the gift before the wreck.
Write it down before it is wrong.
My wrist hurts from the wreck.
Do not wrap the wrong wrist.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: In some words, t goes silent right after s, as in "listen" and "often." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When b follows m at the end of a word, it stays silent, as in "comb" and "thumb." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: L often goes silent before f, k, m, or v, as in "calf," "walk," and "calm." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a word, se can say /z/ instead of /s/, as in "cheese" and "choose." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentences: Choose the cheese
please.
I chose a rose and a pose.
Do not tease the wise rose.
Please choose wisely and pose nicely.
The wise cat chose the cheese
please.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: A final -le pairs a consonant with a quiet vowel sound to close out a word, as in "apple" and "table." Say each word out loud and listen for that last syllable.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: At the end of a word, tion says /shun/, as in "station" and "nation." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: Sion also says /shun/, just like tion, as in "mission" and "session." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: After a base word that ends in d or t, the ending -ed adds a whole new syllable, /ed/, as in "added" and "wanted." Say each word out loud and listen for the extra beat.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: After most other sounds, -ed is said simply as /d/, with no extra syllable, as in "played" and "called." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.

lessons.introText: When a syllable ends in a vowel with nothing after it, that vowel is "open" and usually says its own long name, as in "baker" and "paper." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sentenceWrite.prompt: Write 2 sentences using the words above.
